reference_title: Standard Practice Manual for Flexible Pavements

sections.title: Recycled Asphalt Mixtures
sections.summary: Recycled asphalt mixtures are addressed as a miscellaneous mixture type alongside sand-asphalt, sheet asphalt, rock asphalt, cold-mix, and road-mix pavements, but this UFC does not itself contain the recycling design/construction procedures -- it directs the reader to the dedicated companion document, UFC 3-250-07, for that content.
sections.body: See UFC 3-250-07.
key_points: Recycled asphalt mixtures are one of the miscellaneous mixture types listed in this chapter
Full recycled-asphalt design and construction guidance is contained in the companion document UFC 3-250-07, not in this UFC
sections.applicability: Consult when recycled asphalt materials (reclaimed asphalt pavement) are being considered for a flexible pavement project; refer to UFC 3-250-07 for design/construction detail.

sections.title: Sand-Asphalt Mixtures
sections.summary: In coastal or other regions where clean, angular sand is the only good local aggregate, sand-asphalt mixtures serve as an economical base or surface course for light-load roads/streets; mineral filler is often added for density/stability (but omitted for stabilized base courses), and any of asphalt cement, cutback, or emulsified asphalt is used as binder, mixed cold at a central/travel plant or in place, or hot at a central plant.
sections.body: In regions such as coastal areas where sand of good quality (clean and angular) is the only local aggregate available, the sand is used to produce an economical base or surface course. Sand mixtures, produced from these clean angular sands, are considered for paving roads and streets where light loads are anticipated and where considerable savings are realized by using locally available sand. Mineral filler is often added to increase the density and stability of the mixture, but mineral filler is omitted in designing sand-asphalt mixtures for asphalt-stabilized base courses. Asphalt cement, cutback asphalt, or emulsified asphalt is used for binder. Cold-laid asphalt mixtures are mixed at a central plant, mixed with a travel plant, or mixed in place. HMA is mixed at a central plant. Sand mixes are fine textured, dense, and relatively impermeable. The stability and durability of the sand mixes depend on the quality and grading of the fine aggregate, the amount and grade of asphalt binder, and the degree of control exercised in construction operations. Ensure the sand is sufficiently well-graded to meet the specified aggregate requirements for the type of course to be constructed and is free from excessive amounts of foreign matter. In many cases, the design gradation is obtained by selecting and blending locally available sands.
key_points: Used where clean, angular sand is the only good local aggregate (e.g., coastal areas) for an economical base/surface course under light loads
Mineral filler is often added for density/stability, but is omitted when designing sand-asphalt mixtures for asphalt-stabilized base courses
Binder is asphalt cement, cutback, or emulsified asphalt; cold-laid mixes come from a central plant, travel plant, or in-place mixing, while HMA is central-plant mixed
Sand mixes are fine textured, dense, and relatively impermeable; stability/durability depend on fine-aggregate quality/grading, binder amount/grade, and construction control
Design gradation is often obtained by selecting and blending locally available sands, kept well-graded and free of excessive foreign matter
sections.applicability: Applies where clean angular sand is the only economical local aggregate for a light-traffic road or street base/surface course.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
sections.summary: Sand-asphalt mixes are attractive for their low cost using locally available materials, but their use is limited by relatively low strength and durability, and they typically require a relatively high asphalt content, which raises overall mixture cost.
sections.body: Sand-asphalt mixes are produced with locally available materials at a relatively low cost; however, the use of sand mixes is limited due to their relative lack of strength and durability. Sand asphalt mixtures normally require a relatively high asphalt content thus resulting in a high mixture cost.
key_points: Advantage: low cost from use of locally available materials
Disadvantage: relative lack of strength and durability limits use
Disadvantage: normally requires a relatively high asphalt content, raising mixture cost
sections.applicability: Applies when weighing whether a sand-asphalt mix is an appropriate low-cost alternative for a given project's structural and traffic demands.

sections.title: Uses
sections.summary: Sand mixes are excluded from surface/intermediate courses under high-pressure or solid-rubber/steel/tracked-vehicle traffic (including high-pressure truck and ATV tires), but are considered for asphalt-stabilized base courses under any traffic, for any course in non-traffic areas, and for surface/intermediate courses under low-pressure tires (690 kPa/100 psi or less) and low traffic volumes with trial mixes tested.
sections.body: Sand mixes are not to be used as surface or intermediate courses for airfield and heliport pavements designed for high-pressure tires or for pavements designed for solid-rubber tires, steel wheels, or tracked vehicles. High-pressure truck tires and all-terrain vehicle (ATV) tires are not to be allowed on sand-asphalt mixes. Sand mixes are considered for asphalt-stabilized base courses for all types of traffic areas and for any course in non-traffic areas. Sand mixes are considered for surface and intermediate courses for pavements subjected to low-pressure tires (690 kilopascals (100 psi) or less) and low traffic volumes. In this case, make and test trial mixes in the laboratory. Sand-asphalt mixes have been used to provide temporary travel paths for construction vehicles over completed AC pavements. Ensure the maximum sized aggregate particle are 9.5 millimeters (3/8 inch) or less to prevent the traffic from making indentations on the underlying AC pavement.
key_points: Prohibited as surface/intermediate courses for airfield/heliport pavements under high-pressure tires, solid-rubber tires, steel wheels, or tracked vehicles; high-pressure truck and ATV tires excluded
Allowed for asphalt-stabilized base courses under any traffic area and for any course in non-traffic areas
Allowed for surface/intermediate courses under low-pressure tires (690 kPa / 100 psi or less) and low traffic volumes, with laboratory trial mixes required
Used for temporary construction-vehicle travel paths over completed AC pavements, with max aggregate size 9.5 mm (3/8 in.) to avoid indenting the underlying pavement
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a course type and traffic category for which a sand-asphalt mix is permitted.

sections.title: Sheet Asphalt
sections.summary: Sheet asphalt is a refined hot sand-asphalt pavement with carefully controlled sand grading/quality, mineral filler amount, and asphalt cement content (higher asphalt percentage than plain sand asphalt); it gives a smooth, impermeable, homogeneous surface course best suited to evenly spread traffic and is normally built 38-50 mm (1.5-2 in.) thick over an intermediate course.
sections.body: Sheet asphalt is a refined type of hot sand-asphalt pavement in which the grading, quality of sand, amount of mineral filler, and asphalt cement content are carefully controlled. The percentage of asphalt required is higher than that used for sand asphalt. Sheet asphalt provides a smooth, impermeable, homogeneous surface course that gives the best service when traffic is spread evenly over the pavement. Normally, sheet asphalt is used for surface courses only and is constructed 38 to 50 millimeters (1½ to 2 inches) thick over an intermediate course.
key_points: Refined hot sand-asphalt pavement with tightly controlled sand grading/quality, mineral filler content, and asphalt cement content
Requires a higher asphalt percentage than plain sand asphalt
Produces a smooth, impermeable, homogeneous surface course, best suited to evenly distributed traffic
Used for surface courses only, typically 38-50 mm (1.5-2 in.) thick over an intermediate course
sections.applicability: Applies when a smooth, impermeable surface course is needed and traffic loading is spread evenly rather than channelized.

sections.title: Rock Asphalt
sections.summary: Rock asphalt pavement is crushed natural asphalt-impregnated limestone and/or sandstone, used alone or with added asphalt/flux oil, laid cold like other cold-laid mixtures; it is limited to surface courses on roads (37.5-50.0 mm/1.5-2 in. thick, blended vs. fluxed), sourced from natural deposits in states such as Kentucky, Alabama, Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Utah, and enriched with added asphalt as needed to meet design content.
sections.body: Rock asphalt pavement is composed of crushed, natural asphalt-impregnated limestone or sandstone, or a combination of these, used alone or mixed with additional asphalt or flux oil. Rock asphalt pavement is laid cold in the same manner as cold-laid asphalt mixture. Rock asphalt is used only in surface courses for roads and are not to be constructed over 37.5 and 50.0 millimeters (1½ and 2 inches) thick for blended and fluxed rock-asphalt, respectively. Kentucky, Alabama, Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma and Utah have natural rock-asphalt deposits where paving material is produced commercially. The character and quantity of the aggregate and asphalt in the material vary among the different deposits and vary within the same deposit. Rock asphalt pavement is prepared by blending into the natural asphalt a crushed impregnated limestone or sandstone or a combination of the two in proportions to produce a properly graded mixture with a specified asphalt content. Ensure the natural rock asphalt is enriched (that is, add more asphalt to the mixture) if the material does not contain asphalt in its natural state to produce a mixture meeting design requirements. Hot mixes are produced by heating crushed limestone impregnated with relatively hard asphalt, alone or with added sand, and mixing with additional asphalt cement in a conventional plant.
key_points: Crushed natural asphalt-impregnated limestone and/or sandstone, used alone or with added asphalt/flux oil; laid cold like other cold-laid mixtures
Used only in surface courses for roads; thickness capped at 37.5 mm (1.5 in.) blended and 50.0 mm (2 in.) fluxed rock-asphalt
Commercial natural deposits occur in Kentucky, Alabama, Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Utah; aggregate/asphalt character varies between and within deposits
Natural rock asphalt is enriched with added asphalt if it lacks sufficient natural asphalt content to meet design requirements
Hot mixes are made by heating impregnated crushed limestone (with or without added sand) and mixing with additional asphalt cement in a conventional plant
sections.applicability: Applies to road surface courses in regions with access to natural rock-asphalt deposits.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
sections.summary: Rock asphalt shares the same advantages and disadvantages as plant-mix cold-laid asphalt mixtures, with the added benefit that its cost is reduced because the material already contains binder within the natural rock-asphalt deposit.
sections.body: The advantages and disadvantages are the same as those for plant-mix cold-laid asphalt mixtures. In addition, the use of rock asphalt pavement reduces cost because this mixture already contains binder material.
key_points: Shares the same advantages/disadvantages as plant-mix cold-laid asphalt mixtures
Added advantage: reduced cost because the natural material already contains binder
sections.applicability: Applies when comparing rock asphalt against other cold-laid mixture options on a cost/performance basis.

sections.title: Uses
sections.summary: Rock asphalt pavements are used for roads and streets not subjected to tracked-vehicle traffic, and as slurry-seal aggregate -- but only predominantly sandstone rock asphalts should be used in slurry, since limestone rock asphalts polish under traffic and produce a slick surface.
sections.body: Rock asphalt pavements are used for roads and streets not subjected to traffic by tracked vehicles. Rock asphalts are used as the aggregate in slurry seals, but only use predominantly sandstone rock asphalts in slurry since limestone rock asphalts polish under traffic and thus produce a slick pavement surface.
key_points: Used for roads/streets not subjected to tracked-vehicle traffic
Used as slurry-seal aggregate, but only predominantly sandstone rock asphalts -- limestone rock asphalts polish under traffic and create a slick surface
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a rock-asphalt source for road/street pavement or slurry-seal aggregate, and tracked-vehicle traffic or skid resistance is a concern.

sections.title: Cold-Mix Asphalt
sections.summary: Cold-mix asphalt is a low-cost surface for low-volume roads or a base course for high-volume roads/airfields; it does not match hot-mix quality but performs adequately, can be stored for months (useful for patching) at lower cost since no fuel is needed for heating, though it typically reaches lower density than hot mix and needs a curing period for volatiles/water to evaporate before it gains shear strength.
sections.body: Cold-mix asphalt pavements are used as a low-cost surface for low-volume roads or as a base course for high-volume roads and airfields. While cold mixes do not provide pavements with the same quality as hot mixes, cold mixes do perform for the purposes intended. Cold mixes are capable of being stored for several months and are useful for patching. Because fuel is not needed to heat cold mixes, these pavements are constructed at lower cost than hot mixes. Two disadvantages of using cold mixes are that usually a lower density is obtained in cold mixes than in the construction of hot mixes and that a curing period is needed to allow water or volatiles to evaporate so that shear strength is obtained.
key_points: Low-cost surface for low-volume roads, or base course for high-volume roads and airfields
Lower quality than hot mixes but adequate for intended purposes; storable for several months and useful for patching
Lower cost than hot mix because no fuel is needed for heating
Disadvantages: typically lower achieved density than hot mix, and a curing period is needed for water/volatiles to evaporate before shear strength develops
sections.applicability: Applies where a low-cost, storable asphalt mixture is acceptable for low-volume road surfaces or as a base course, and immediate high density/strength is not required.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: Frames the cold-mix design process addressed by this section's subsections: a preliminary materials/quantity survey (6-5.1.1), aggregate and asphalt-cement testing (6-5.1.2), and the laboratory procedure for determining optimum asphalt cement content (6-5.1.3), applicable specifically to dense-graded cold-mix pavements.
key_points: Cold-mix design proceeds through a preliminary materials survey, aggregate/asphalt testing, and optimum-asphalt-content determination
The design procedure covered in this section applies only to dense-graded cold-mix pavements
sections.applicability: Applies when developing a dense-graded cold-mix asphalt paving mixture design.

sections.title: Preliminary Work
sections.summary: The first design step is a survey confirming needed materials (coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, mineral filler, bitumen) are available in sufficient quantity and economical to use, with sampling per the section's requirements; test reports document aggregate/bituminous sampling and gradation analysis, with quantities sufficient for ASTM and laboratory pavement-design testing (normally about 90 kg/200 lb of desired-gradation aggregate and 19 L/5 gal of bitumen).
sections.body: The first step in designing a paving mixture is to make a survey to ensure that the materials needed are available in quantities meeting job requirements and their use is economical in the pavement construction. Obtain sufficient samples of material during the survey to accomplish the tests described in this section of this UFC. Materials normally required for the paving mix are coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, mineral filler, and bitumen. Sampling: Test reports reflecting the results of sampling and testing of the aggregates and bituminous materials are prepared. Conduct a gradation analysis on the aggregates to determine whether the aggregates when blended meet the contract gradation specifications. Furnish representative samples of materials for laboratory testing. Divide samples into sizes meeting testing requirements in the laboratory, in a way that represents field conditions. Sufficient quantities of materials are obtained at the time of sampling to meet the ASTM requirements and for laboratory pavement design tests described in this section of this UFC. Normally, aggregates that produces 90 kilograms (200 pounds) of the desired gradation and 19 liters (5 gallons) of bitumen is sufficient for these tests.
key_points: First step: survey to confirm needed materials (coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, mineral filler, bitumen) are available in adequate, economical quantity
Sampling: prepare test reports on aggregate/bituminous sampling and testing; run gradation analysis to confirm blended aggregates meet contract specifications
Divide representative samples into laboratory testing sizes that reflect field conditions
Typical sample quantities: about 90 kg (200 lb) of desired-gradation aggregate and 19 L (5 gal) of bitumen, sufficient for ASTM and laboratory pavement-design tests
sections.applicability: Applies at the start of a cold-mix design effort, before laboratory testing of aggregate and asphalt cement begins.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Covers aggregate and asphalt-cement testing for cold-mix design: aggregates must be clean, hard, durable, and angular for stability, with Table 6-1 giving typical dense- and open-graded gradation limits; asphalt-cement testing establishes specific gravity per ASTM D402/D244/D70, and Table 6-2 guides asphalt type/grade selection by climatic condition and whether the mix is used immediately or stockpiled.
sections.body: Tests on Aggregates: Ensure aggregates for use in an asphalt mixture are clean, hard, and durable. Angular aggregates provide an increased stability in pavements compared to rounded aggregates. Tests of aggregates required in the design of HMA mixtures are also applicable to the cold-mix type. Table 6-1 lists typical aggregate gradation requirements for both dense- and open-graded mixtures. The gradation used depends on the application and the binder. Dense-graded mixtures are used in most applications; open-graded mixtures provide more workability in colder weather. Many proprietary cold-patch materials use an open grading along with a modified binder. The dense-graded aggregate gradations correspond to those recommended in this text for hot-mix, hot-laid asphalt mixtures, which are provided in Table 2-1 for HMA. Generally, combine aggregates for paving mixes from a minimum of two stockpiles. Mathematical equations are available for making such combinations but are not presented in this UFC because they are lengthy and because trial-and-error procedures are normally easier. The method of combining stockpile sample gradations is described in section 2-4 on dense-graded HMA. Ensure the gradation of the aggregate falls within the limits of the gradation for the project specifications, such as those provided in Table 6-1. Ensure the final gradation presents a smooth curve when plotted with sieve size versus percent passing. Tests on Asphalt Cement: Know the specific gravity of the asphalt cement to determine the percent by volume of bituminous materials in the mix. Because only the residual asphalt is used in calculating the percent binder, the amount of residual asphalt cement in cutback asphalts and asphalt emulsions are determined as specified in ASTM D402 and ASTM D244 for cutback and emulsified asphalts, respectively. Determine the specific gravity of the residual asphalt as described in ASTM D70. In addition to cutback asphalts and emulsified asphalts, cold-mix asphalt pavements are made with asphalt cement and liquefier (cutback) produced to meet a project's design requirements. This cutback asphalt is produced, usually for remote projects, by using kerosene to liquefy an asphalt cement; the type of asphalt cement used is varied easily to meet various climate conditions, and the cutback binder produced has a relatively long shelf life depending on the amount of kerosene added. Asphalt emulsions are advantageous in that damp aggregate is allowed to be used in the mixing process, whereas dry aggregates are required for the other binder materials; mixes made with asphalt emulsions normally cannot be stockpiled unless the emulsion has been specifically formulated for stockpiling. Table 6-2 provides a guide to the selection of the type and grade of asphalt cement, based on climatic conditions during construction or storage (cold, moderate, or hot) and on whether the mix is to be used immediately or stockpiled for later use.
key_points: Aggregates must be clean, hard, and durable; angular aggregates give increased stability versus rounded aggregates
Table 6-1: typical dense- and open-graded aggregate gradation requirements -- dense-graded for most applications, open-graded for greater cold-weather workability
Combine aggregates from a minimum of two stockpiles by trial-and-error (no combination equations are presented in this UFC); final gradation should plot as a smooth curve
Asphalt-cement specific gravity is determined per ASTM D402 (cutback residual asphalt), ASTM D244 (emulsion residual asphalt), and ASTM D70 (residual asphalt specific gravity)

Kerosene-cutback asphalt cement is used for remote projects, offering climate-adjustable grade and shelf life depending on kerosene content; emulsions allow damp-aggregate mixing but usually cannot be stockpiled unless specially formulated
Table 6-2: asphalt type/grade selection by climatic condition (cold/moderate/hot) and by immediate-use vs. stockpile use
tables: Table 6-1: Typical Aggregate Gradations for Plant-Mix Cold-Laid Asphalt Mixtures
Table 6-2: Selection of Asphalt Type and Grade
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and qualifying the aggregate gradation and asphalt cement type/grade for a cold-mix design.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: Describes the dense-graded cold-mix asphalt-content design procedure (per CRD-C 649/650, Asphalt Institute MS-14/MS-19 guidance): test a minimum of five trial asphalt contents bracketing the estimated optimum, proportion stockpiled aggregates to the target gradation, then take the optimum asphalt content as the average of the contents meeting Table 6-3's unit-weight, VTM, and VFA criteria, corrected for residual asphalt and reduced slightly for incomplete volatile evaporation.
sections.body: The following procedure is recommended for determining the amount of asphalt cement to be used in the paving mix for cold-mix pavements. This procedure is applicable only for dense-graded mixtures. This design procedure is similar to the procedure used for designing HMA mixes for roads and streets. Laboratory equipment and test procedures are required to conform to CRD-C 649 and CRD-C 650. There is no widely accepted standard method for the design of all types of cold mixes. The Asphalt Institute provides information on design and construction procedures for cold mixes in MS-14; information specific to emulsions is available in MS-19. Base the selection of the design method on past experience and local practices. Asphalt Contents for Specimens: the quantity of asphalt cement required for an aggregate is an important factor in mixture design; to start the laboratory tests, make an estimate of the optimum asphalt cement content for the aggregate to be tested. Laboratory tests normally are conducted for a minimum of five asphalt cement contents: two above, two below, and one at the estimated optimum content. Incremental changes of 1 percent are used for preliminary work, but increments of 0.5 percent are used where the optimum asphalt cement content is known and for final designs. Proportioning of Aggregates: as a preliminary step in mixture design and manufacture, determine the proportions of the different available stockpiled materials required to produce the desired gradation of aggregate. This step determines whether a blend is produced meeting design requirements and, if so, the proportion of aggregates to be fed from the cold feeders into the dryer. Sieve analyses are conducted on material from each of the stockpiles, and the aggregates are combined as described in CHAPTER 2. After a blend has been prepared from the available materials meeting design requirements, samples of these materials are processed for use in the laboratory design tests as specified in CRD-C 649. Determination of Optimum Asphalt Cement Content: the optimum asphalt cement content is taken as the average of the asphalt contents corresponding to the mix properties in Table 6-3 (the source text's cross-reference reads "Table 6-7", but the table immediately following this discussion is printed as Table 6-3, Selection of Optimum Asphalt Content). The optimum asphalt cement content is the amount of asphalt cement that is incorporated into the mix. The percent of cutback asphalts and emulsified asphalts are corrected to give a residual asphalt content equal to the optimum asphalt content determined by the tests. Because all of the volatiles do not evaporate, decrease slightly the amount of bitumen to be added as determined by this mix design procedure. When the asphalt cement and kerosene-type mix is to be used, add the desired amount of kerosene to the actual paving mix in addition to the optimum asphalt content determined from the laboratory design.
key_points: Design procedure applies only to dense-graded cold-mix pavements; laboratory equipment/procedures conform to CRD-C 649 and CRD-C 650
No single accepted standard method for all cold mixes; Asphalt Institute MS-14 (general cold mixes) and MS-19 (emulsions) provide guidance, selected per past experience/local practice
Test a minimum of five trial asphalt contents (two above, two below, one at estimated optimum): 1 percent increments for preliminary work, 0.5 percent for final design
Proportion stockpiled aggregates to the target gradation via sieve analysis before processing laboratory design samples per CRD-C 649
Table 6-3: optimum asphalt content taken as the average of contents meeting the unit-weight (peak of curve), VTM (4+/-1 percent), and VFA (75+/-5 percent) criteria
Residual asphalt content is corrected for cutback/emulsion percentage and reduced slightly since not all volatiles evaporate; kerosene is added separately for kerosene-cutback mixes
tables: Table 6-3: Selection of Optimum Asphalt Content
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the optimum asphalt cement content for a dense-graded cold-mix paving mixture in the laboratory.

sections.title: Plant Mix
sections.summary: Introduces plant-produced cold-mix asphalt: producing the mixture in a plant (versus mixing in place in the field) increases quality control, yielding much tighter gradation and binder-content control, though overall costs are greater than in-place mixing.
sections.body: Quality control is increased for mixtures produced in a plant Vs mixtures mixed in place in the field. This increased control results in a much tighter gradation and binder content control, although overall costs are greater compared to in-place mixing.
key_points: Plant production gives tighter gradation and binder-content control than in-place (road) mixing
Increased quality control comes at greater overall cost compared to in-place mixing
sections.applicability: Applies when comparing plant-mix versus in-place (road-mix) cold-mix production for a given project's quality and cost requirements.

sections.title: Plant Operation
sections.summary: Plant operation varies by binder type: kerosene and asphalt cement are introduced onto the aggregate at different times for kerosene-cutback mixes, drying is not required for emulsions but aggregates are heated for cutback binders (capped at 93 C/200 F for RC cutbacks, 121 C/250 F for MC grades or kerosene-cutback), and Table 6-4 gives the required pugmill-introduction temperature ranges by material and grade.
sections.body: The plant operation varies with the type of asphalt material used in the mix. For mixes using asphalt cement and kerosene, introduce the kerosene and asphalt cement onto the aggregate at different times. Drying of the aggregate is not a design requirement with asphalt emulsions, but for cutback binders, heat the aggregates. Ensure aggregates are not hotter than 93 degrees C (200 degrees F) when mixed with RC cutback asphalts and not hotter than 121 degrees C (250 degrees F) for mixing with MC grades or asphalt cement and kerosene. Ensure the asphalt materials are in the temperature ranges provided in Table 6-4 (the source text's cross-reference reads "Table 6-8", but the table immediately following this discussion is printed as Table 6-4, Mixing Temperatures for Asphalt Materials) when introduced into the pugmill.
key_points: Kerosene-cutback mixes: introduce kerosene and asphalt cement onto the aggregate at different times
Aggregate drying not required with asphalt emulsions; aggregates are heated for cutback binders
Maximum aggregate temperature: 93 C (200 F) for RC cutback asphalts; 121 C (250 F) for MC grades or asphalt cement/kerosene mixes
Table 6-4 gives the required asphalt-material temperature ranges at pugmill introduction, by material type and grade
tables: Table 6-4: Mixing Temperatures for Asphalt Materials
sections.applicability: Applies when operating a cold-mix asphalt plant, to set aggregate heating and binder introduction practice by binder type.

sections.title: Plant Laboratory
sections.summary: A plant laboratory verifies aggregate gradation and asphalt-material content against design requirements using a mechanical sieve shaker and full sets of standard sieves (12.5 mm to 75 micrometer, per ASTM E11), a bitumen-content extractor or ignition test, a 2 kg precision balance, and Marshall compaction/testing equipment.
sections.body: Use of a plant laboratory ensures that the aggregate meets design gradation requirements and that the mix contains the prescribed percentage of asphalt material. The plant laboratory contains this major equipment: a. A hand- or power-driven mechanical sieve shaker. The sieve shaker is required to have a capacity of not less than eight full-height, 200-millimeter (8-inch) -diameter sieves. b. A full-height, 200-millimeter (8-inch) -diameter sieve for each of the following sieve openings: 12.5 millimeter (1/2 inch), 9.5 millimeter (3/8 inch), 4.75 millimeter (No. 4), 2.36 millimeter (No. 8), 1.18 millimeter (No. 16), 600 micrometer (No. 30), 300 micrometer (No. 50), 150 micrometer (No. 100), and 75 micrometer (No. 200). The sieves are required to have square openings and conform to the requirements of ASTM E11. c. An extractor or ignition test for measuring bitumen content within close tolerances. d. A balance having a capacity of 2 kilograms (4.4 pounds) and sensitive to 0.1 gram (0.0035 ounce). e. Marshall equipment for compacting and testing samples to verify mixture design.
key_points: Purpose: confirm aggregate meets design gradation and mix contains the prescribed asphalt percentage
Mechanical sieve shaker with capacity for at least eight full-height, 200 mm (8 in.) sieves
Full sieve set from 12.5 mm (1/2 in.) down to 75 micrometer (No. 200), conforming to ASTM E11
Bitumen-content extractor or ignition test, and a 2 kg (4.4 lb) balance sensitive to 0.1 g (0.0035 oz)
Marshall equipment for compacting and testing samples to verify mixture design
sections.applicability: Applies to equipping and operating the quality-control laboratory at a cold-mix asphalt plant.

sections.title: Adjusting Mix Proportions
sections.summary: Mix proportions are adjusted whenever tests show tolerances are not met; automated plants are consistent when properly calibrated, and weighing variations/faulty scales are caught by monitoring load weights, keeping each load's total weight within plus or minus 2 percent of the batch weights dumped into the truck.
sections.body: Adjust mix proportions whenever tests indicate that specified tolerances are not being met. Fully automated plants produce consistent mixtures, provided that the equipment is calibrated and in good working condition. Variations in weighing techniques or faulty scales are detected readily and corrective measures taken by maintaining a close check on load weights. Ensure the total weight of each load of mixture produced only varies between plus or minus 2 percent from the total of the batch weights dumped into the truck.
key_points: Adjust mix proportions when tests show specified tolerances are not met
Automated plants are consistent only if properly calibrated and maintained
Monitor load weights to detect weighing-technique variation or faulty scales
Each load's total weight must stay within plus or minus 2 percent of the summed batch weights
sections.applicability: Applies during plant production, as an ongoing quality-control check on batch weights and mix proportioning.

sections.title: Preparation of Construction Specifications
sections.summary: Covers the specification/placement/compaction workflow for plant-mix cold-laid pavements: guide specifications normally govern except for limited repair quantities under 100 metric tons (needing Pavements DWG coordination or approval above that threshold); placement favors a motor grader for spreading and mix aeration; and compaction timing depends on the mixture reaching the specified cohesion, avoiding both instability under the roller and excessive stiffness.
sections.body: Specifications: Cold-laid asphalt mixtures are produced according to the provisions of guide specifications except when mix quantities, less than 100 metric tons (100 tons), are specified for limited use in repairs. In these cases, the procedures specified in the guide specification are not economical. When such an exception is allowed, locally available cold-laid bituminous mix produced according to local state highway department specifications are used. Contact the Pavements Discipline Working Group (DWG) or their designated representative for these exceptions. When the quantity equals or exceeds 100 metric tons (100 tons), approval from the Pavements DWG or their designated representative is required. Provide a copy of the specification or reference thereto and information regarding traffic conditions and facilities to be paved to facilitate discussions. Placing: Although closer control of layer thickness and better prevention of segregation of the mix is achieved with a mechanical spreader, a motor grader is desirable for spreading plant-mix cold-laid pavements. Aeration of the mix to remove volatile material is often required to bring the mix to the design condition for compaction. A motor grader aerates the mix by blading it back and forth across the roadbed. Compaction of Mixture: At the time of compaction, the asphalt material in the mixture is required to provide the specified amount of cohesion so that the design density is reached. Cohesion of the mixture is controlled by the type of asphalt material, volatile content, and temperature of the mixture. Low cohesion causes the mix to be unstable under the roller, while high cohesion causes the mix to be too stiff to be compacted. Compact the mixture as soon as it supports the roller without undue displacement.
key_points: Specifications: guide specifications govern except for limited repair quantities under 100 metric tons (100 tons), where local highway-department specifications may apply with Pavements DWG coordination
Quantities at or above 100 metric tons require Pavements DWG (or designated representative) approval, with specification copy and traffic/facility information provided

Placing: a motor grader is desirable for spreading, though a mechanical spreader gives closer thickness control and better segregation prevention; grader blading also aerates the mix to remove volatiles
Compaction: proceed once the mixture supports the roller without undue displacement -- low cohesion causes instability under the roller, high cohesion makes the mix too stiff to compact
sections.applicability: Applies when writing project specifications and directing field placement/compaction of plant-mix cold-laid asphalt pavements.

sections.title: Road Mix
sections.summary: Asphalt road mixes are mixed in place using travel plants or common road-building equipment (blade graders, disk harrows, drags, pressure distributors) on existing, blended, or imported subgrade/base aggregate; a travel plant gives more accurate proportioning and uniformity than mixed-in-place methods and reduced curing time with viscous cutbacks, while curing removes volatiles/water before spreading and compacting.
sections.body: Asphalt road mixes are normally mixed in place by travel plants or common types of road-building equipment, such as blade graders, disk harrows, drags, and pressure distributors. When allowed by design, the existing subgrade materials, loosened existing subgrade materials blended with imported materials, or properly processed imported materials placed on the existing base or subgrade have been used as aggregate in road mixes. When the amount of material passing the 75 microns (No. 200) sieve exceeds 20 percent, processing with asphalt is difficult and this material benefits from the addition of imported materials. A wide range of aggregates are used, and the gradation requirements are less strict than those for hot or cold plant-mixed types. The bitumen is often applied by a pressure distributor to the processed aggregate on the base or subgrade and then thoroughly mixed with the aggregate. A travel-type mixing plant combines the aggregates with an asphalt material and continuously discharges the mixture at the rear of the machine as the plant travels along the strip being paved. Using a travel plant permits accurate proportioning of the bitumen and aggregate and produces a uniform and higher quality mixture vs. a mixed-in-place method. Further, because viscous types of cutback asphalt are used, the curing time is reduced. Curing is usually required to reduce the volatiles in the cutback asphalt or water in the asphalt emulsion prior to spreading and compacting because excessive amounts of volatiles and water affect the compatibility of the mixture and the stability of the finished pavement. Manipulation with blades or other road machines speed curing.
key_points: Mixed in place using travel plants or common road-building equipment (blade graders, disk harrows, drags, pressure distributors)
Aggregate source: existing subgrade, existing subgrade blended with imported material, or imported material placed on the existing base/subgrade
When material passing the No. 200 (75 micrometer) sieve exceeds 20 percent, asphalt processing is difficult and benefits from imported-material addition
Travel plant gives more accurate bitumen/aggregate proportioning and a more uniform, higher-quality mixture than mixed-in-place, with reduced curing time from viscous cutbacks
Curing (often sped by blading) removes cutback volatiles or emulsion water before spreading/compacting, since excess volatiles/water harm mixture compatibility and finished-pavement stability
sections.applicability: Applies where in-place mixing of an existing or imported subgrade/base aggregate with asphalt binder is used to build a road-mix pavement course.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
sections.summary: Asphalt road mix needs much less equipment than HMA construction and uses locally available materials, giving significant cost savings, but lacks HMA's strength/durability; it is economical for small pavement quantities, subgrade meeting design requirements, or nearby suitable aggregate, and needs seal coats with aggregate cover since road mixes are often open graded/low density.
sections.body: Much less equipment is required for construction using asphalt road mix than is required using AC, thus resulting in cost savings. Using locally available materials also results in significant cost savings. Asphalt road mix, however, does not have the strength or durability of HMA. The road-mix type of pavement provides an economical means of obtaining a surface for roads and streets when the required amount of pavement is small, when the natural soil meets aggregate design requirements, or when aggregates meeting design requirements are nearby. Apply seal coats with aggregate cover as a part of road-mix construction since road mixes are often open graded or of relatively low density and are therefore susceptible to oxidation and abrasion.
key_points: Advantages: much less construction equipment than AC/HMA, plus use of locally available materials -- significant cost savings
Disadvantage: does not have the strength or durability of HMA
Economical when the required pavement quantity is small, the natural soil meets aggregate requirements, or suitable aggregate is nearby
Seal coats with aggregate cover are applied because road mixes are often open graded/low density and susceptible to oxidation and abrasion
sections.applicability: Applies when weighing road mix against other pavement types for small-quantity or locally-sourced-aggregate road/street projects.

sections.title: Uses
sections.summary: Properly designed road mix on a suitable existing subgrade or with local aggregate approaches central-plant cold-mix quality; it is used for intermediate or surface courses but is generally considered inferior to plant mixtures due to less accurate control, is not allowed above the base course on airfields, and serves as a wearing course for temporary roads or the first stage of stage-constructed permanent roads/streets, with seal coats improving durability.
sections.body: When an asphalt road mix is properly designed and constructed on an existing subgrade meeting design requirements or using locally available aggregates, the quality of road-mix construction approaches that of cold mix produced in a central plant. Road mix is used for intermediate or surface courses, but because of the less accurate control, road mix is often considered inferior to plant mixtures. Road mix is not allowed for use above the base course for airfields. Road mix is used as a wearing course for temporary roads and streets or as the first step in stage construction for permanent roads and streets when these are to be supplemented by plant-mix surfaces as the demands of traffic increase and warrant the increased thickness. Seal coats reduce infiltration of air and water and thus improve the durability of road-mix pavements.
key_points: Properly designed/constructed road mix on suitable subgrade or local aggregate approaches central-plant cold-mix quality
Used for intermediate or surface courses, but generally considered inferior to plant mixtures due to less accurate control
Not allowed for use above the base course on airfields
Used as a wearing course for temporary roads/streets, or as the first stage of stage-constructed permanent roads/streets later supplemented by plant-mix surfaces
Seal coats reduce air/water infiltration and improve road-mix pavement durability
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting road mix for temporary roads/streets or as an initial stage-construction course for permanent roads/streets, excluding airfield use above the base course.
